title: The Visitation (31 May)
hookLine: May ends where Mary's traveling began, with Elizabeth

cards: A young woman has just heard news that will change everything. An angel, Luke says, has told her she will bear a son.
In the same breath, the angel mentions her older relative Elizabeth, who was called barren, and who is now with child too. What does she do next? She doesn't sit at home with the secret.
She doesn't wait to be sure. She packs and goes, up into the hill country, to the one other woman who might understand. Today, the last feast of May: the Visitation.

teach.b: Here's how Luke puts it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda." With haste. Mary doesn't drift.
Mary greets Elizabeth, and Luke says the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps.
Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out with a loud voice: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Those words may sound familiar.

Catholics say them in the Hail Mary, after the angel's greeting, so they pray this meeting every time they say it. Notice who is in the room. Two women, one old and one young, both carrying children nobody expected.
No priests, no crowds, no kings. Two relatives in a house in the hills, and the one Luke says leaped for joy is a child not yet born.
Then Mary answers with a song of her own, the one Catholics call the Magnificat and still sing at evening prayer.
And she stays: about three months, Luke says. Not a quick visit and a gift at the door.
Luke doesn't say what filled those months; tradition pictures her helping as Elizabeth's time drew near. That's the shape of the feast. Good news doesn't make Mary sit still.
It sends her out, fast, to someone who needs company, and once she's there, she doesn't hurry away.

how: Catholics keep the feast of the Visitation on 31 May, closing the month Catholic tradition dedicates to Mary; Elizabeth's greeting is prayed in every Hail Mary, and the Magnificat is sung at Evening Prayer.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has just told you your news, and that your relative Elizabeth is expecting too. what do you do?
o: keep it to yourself and wait.
write to Elizabeth when you're ready.
set out at once for the hill country.
games.why: Mary rises up and goes with haste. when she greets Elizabeth, the child leaps in Elizabeth's womb.

practice: Bring to mind someone who might need company right now: someone expecting a child or caring for one, someone older living alone, someone carrying news they haven't told many people.
Notice what has kept you from going, waiting for a better week or for the right words, and picture the soonest real moment you could be with them, phone away, no glance at the clock.
If you pray, say Elizabeth's words, the ones Catholics say in the Hail Mary; if you don't, simply hold that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: The Visitation. Mary's journey into the hill country to visit Elizabeth, where the child leaped and Elizabeth called her blessed.

orig.note: Greek, Luke 1:39: with haste — also with eagerness, earnestness.

carryVoice: Your line: she went in haste. Quick to arrive, and in no hurry to leave. See you tomorrow.
